newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU welcomes British Labour win, Hong Kong unmoved.
newsitem.headline: EU welcomes British Labour win, Hong Kong unmoved.

text.p: Britain's European partners on Friday welcomed the Labour Party's landslide general election victory and expressed hope a new government under Tony Blair would be easier to deal with on European integration.

Farther afield, Asian nations offered congratulations to Blair and his new-look party, but leaders in Hong Kong, which reverts from British to Chinese rule on June 30, were unmoved and focusing on their new masters in Beijing.
Few tears were shed across the EU over John Major's thumping defeat, but the other 14 nations in the group were reluctant to contemplate a relaxation in London on key issues of sovereignty.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, speaking in Brunei during an Asian tour, said the poll showed Britons did not like anti-European polemics, adding anti-EU policies could not win votes anywhere.

Seeking to bask in reflected glory, German Social Democrats (SPD) hailed Blair's win as the start of a trend they hope will return them to power in a federal parliamentary election next year after 16 years in opposition.
German editorial writers were scathing about the defeated Conservatives, whose Eurosceptical and sometimes anti-German campaign offended sensitivities of their readers.
Despite reluctance to give up their mark currency, most Germans see European integration as a lofty ideal and anti-EU sentiments as a slippery slope towards a dangerous nationalism.

In France, which is caught in the throes of campaigning for its own two-stage parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1, President Jacques Chirac said in a message to Blair that he would be happy to meet him soon in the French capital. The invitation was informal and no dates were mentioned.

French European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier said his country's opposition Socialists had yet to understand that their British counterparts had won the election because they had dropped "outmoded precepts" about state control of the economy.

In Amsterdam, a Dutch government press statement said Prime Minister Wim Kok had "congratulated Blair in a telegram and expressed the hope that the new British government will contribute to a positive result at the (EU's) Intergovernmental Conference (IGC) in Amsterdam in June".

In Brussels, EU diplomats said Labour could have an immediate impact at an IGC preparatory meeting on Monday expected to be the last before the Dutch EU presidency puts forward a draft treaty ahead of the Amsterdam summit.

The IGC, due to complete its revision of the Maastricht Treaty on European union by mid-June and streamline the bloc's institutions ahead of an ambitious eastward expansion, has seemed anathema to the Conservatives, who feared federalism and muttered darkly about the threat to the nation-state.

Denmark's leading opposition Liberal party, which is likely to head a centre-right government after elections due by September 1998, said Labour's victory could mean increased pressure on Euro-sceptical Denmark to conform with European Union policies.

In Hong Kong, the colony's last British governor, former Conservative cabinet minister Chris Patten, and the territory's future leader Tung Chee-hwa congratulated Labour leader Tony Blair on his victory, but most political commentators said the election would have little impact in the territory.

In Australia, the nation's opposition Labor Party cheered Blair's win and said his success was in part a result of the lessons he learned from the Australian Labor Party. Conservative Prime Minister John Howard also congratulated Blair, but said his counterpart John Major never stood a chance.

Australian Labor leader Kim Beazley said Blair's victory was a result of his ability to restructure the British Labour Party to make it relevant to the British people after a long period in opposition.
Malaysia said it looked forward to continuing its "excellent relations" with Britain, despite past trade disputes, while Bangladesh said it expected stronger ties.
In Tokyo, the only immediate reaction was to sell sterling, which fell across the board in late trade partly in reaction to fears the Labour Party would like to take a soft sterling policy.
